evidence_quotes.quote: The overarching objective of the activity was to determine if the interventions improved women employees’ perceptions and experiences of managing their periods in the workplace

The MH in the Workplace action research interventions were implemented over a 9–11-month period in four private sector workplaces: two carpet and rug manufacturers in Nepal (Nepal Companies A and B), a textile manufacturer in Kenya (Kenya Company A), and a garment manufacturer in Kenya (Kenya Company B).
Over 9–11 months, interventions focused on (i) menstrual products and WASH infrastructure; (ii) workplace policy environment; and (iii) education and behavior change.
In addition, reviews of the workplace policies were conducted at each company with the aim of contributing to a more supportive workplace environment for menstruating employees.
The ﬁrst research question was investigated using data collected from a mixed methods approach at baseline and endline.
After the intervention, the number and cleanliness of toilets improved in all four workplaces; however, changes were not uniform, nor did access increase for all staff.

criterion_notes.c1: No. The study examines private-sector workplace menstrual health and hygiene (MH/MHM) for manufacturing employees in four factories in Kenya and Nepal (focusing on menstrual product provision, menstrual education/stigma reduction, workplace leave/support, and employee washroom cleanliness/amenities), rather than household or community water or sanitation service access. Although the two Nepali carpet factories had on-site residential facilities where employees and families lived and worked, the study focuses on managing menstruation on the job rather than household or community water or sanitation service access.
criterion_notes.c2: No under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading; borderline/partial on plain wording alone, though overall decision remains exclude under both readings. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 clarification, the exposure is a bundled donor-funded (USAID WASHPaLS) workplace MHM project combining generic project delivery (free menstrual pads/cups and company-funded toilet repairs), behavioural promotion (Appreciative Inquiry and MHH education/BCC), and general private-company HR policy reviews/recommendations (flexible hours/menstrual leave and supervisor sensitization), rather than an isolated legal, regulatory, or administrative rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community water or sanitation service access. Under the literal/plain broad wording of Criterion 2, internal company 'workplace policy environment' reviews and supervisory practices around leave or toilet breaks could arguably qualify as an institutional or administrative workplace factor, though their effects are not separated from free pad distribution and BCC; even granting plain Criterion 2, the study is still excluded because it fails Criterion 1 (workplace MHM rather than household/community water or sanitation service access) and Criterion 4 (no water or sanitation service access outcome).
criterion_notes.c3: Yes. Contains primary empirical evidence from a pre-post mixed-methods pilot/action-research evaluation across four workplaces using baseline and endline employee questionnaires, workplace infrastructure assessments, focus group discussions (FGDs), and key informant interviews (KIIs).
criterion_notes.c4: No. Quantitative outcomes (Tables 3-10) measure menstrual knowledge, self-confidence managing periods at work, access to and comfort/cleanliness of personal menstrual materials (pads/cups), workplace social support and comfort requesting menstrual leave, menstruation-related absenteeism, self-rated work quality, and job satisfaction. Questions on facilities were removed from the endline survey, with only a brief narrative facility-audit note that workplace toilet numbers and cleanliness improved unevenly and access did not increase for all staff. No household or community water or sanitation service access outcome is reported.
criterion_notes.c5: Yes. Population and units of analysis (individual factory employees and workplaces across four companies in Nepal and Kenya), the bundled workplace MH intervention exposure, the MH and workplace/business outcomes, and the uncontrolled pre-post mixed-methods action-research design are all clearly reported.
criterion_notes.c6: Yes. Full text is in English.

study_design: Uncontrolled pre–post mixed-methods pilot / action-research study
population_and_sample: Employees, supervisors, and managers at four private manufacturing companies: Nepal Company A (52 women employees at baseline, 58 at endline; 124 total staff), Nepal Company B (67 women employees at baseline, 63 at endline; 96 total staff), Kenya Company A (51 women and 550 men at baseline, 73 women at endline), and Kenya Company B (259 women and 87 men at baseline, 281 women and 113 men at endline). Units of analysis: individual employee and workplace.
exposure: A 5-to-11-month USAID WASHPaLS bundled workplace menstrual health (MH) intervention across four private firms comprising (i) free menstrual product provision (pads, menstrual cups, underwear) and workplace WASH toilet assessments/upgrades, (ii) company workplace policy reviews/recommendations and leadership sensitization, and (iii) menstrual health education and behavior change communication (Appreciative Inquiry, videos, in-person sessions).
outcome: Menstrual knowledge, confidence in managing menstruation at work, access to and comfort/cleanliness of menstrual materials, perceived colleague/supervisory support and comfort requesting menstruation-related leave, menstruation-related absenteeism, self-rated work quality during menstruation, job satisfaction, and narrative facility-audit observations on workplace toilet cleanliness and numbers.
rationale: Excluded (E01 - Wrong topic). This study evaluates a USAID WASHPaLS private-sector workplace menstrual health (MH) pilot program across four manufacturing factories in Kenya and Nepal aimed at improving menstrual management on the job, women's economic empowerment, and business outcomes. It fails Criterion 1 because it studies private-sector workplace menstrual health management (menstrual pad/cup provision, MHH education, menstrual stigma/leave, and factory washroom upgrades) rather than household or community water or sanitation service access. It also fails Criterion 2 under the 2026-10-13 clarification because it evaluates a bundled NGO project-delivery and behavioural-promotion intervention (free products, BCC/Appreciative Inquiry, toilet repairs, and general internal HR policy recommendations) rather than a rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing water or sanitation service access, and fails Criterion 4 because its measured outcomes concern menstrual knowledge, pad comfort/supply, workplace support/leave, absenteeism, work performance, and job satisfaction (with facility items dropped from the endline survey). Even under the plain broad reading of Criterion 2, the paper remains excluded on Criteria 1 and 4.
